result: Conditioned media from p63-expressing PDA cell lines (BxPC3, T3M4, KLM1) induced a distinct transcriptional response in pancreatic stellate cells (PSCs) characterized by inflammatory gene expression, increased proliferation, and enrichment of the iCAF signature.
evaluation: Claims C12-C15 are supported by RNA-seq data showing clustering of PSCs treated with conditioned media from p63-expressing cell lines (Figure 1E), GSEA analysis demonstrating iCAF signature enrichment (Figure 1H), and proliferation assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C). The experimental design is appropriate and the data converge to support the conclusion.

result: p63 expression in PDA cells is necessary and sufficient to drive iCAF marker induction and suppress myCAF markers in PSCs through a secretory phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C17-C20 are supported by gain-of-function experiments (SUIT2-p63, mM1-p63) and loss-of-function experiments (KLM1 p63 knockout) showing consistent changes in iCAF and myCAF markers by RT-qPCR (Figures 2B-I). The bidirectional genetic manipulation provides strong evidence for causality.

result: Ectopic p63 expression in SUIT2 cells enhances tumor growth in vivo but not in vitro, and promotes iCAF enrichment, neutrophil infiltration, and systemic inflammation in the tumor microenvironment.
evaluation: Claims C21-C24 are supported by in vivo tumor growth measurements (Figure 3A-B), RNA-seq analysis showing iCAF signature enrichment (Figure 3G), flow cytometry demonstrating increased neutrophil infiltration (Figure 3H-I), and ELISA showing elevated plasma IL-6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1U). The in vivo-specific growth phenotype is validated in multiple models.

result: p63 inactivation in KLM1 cells reduces tumor growth in vivo and suppresses inflammatory transcriptional signatures in both the fibroblast and immune compartments of the tumor stroma.
evaluation: Claims C25-C27 are supported by bioluminescence imaging showing reduced tumor growth (Figure 4A-B), RNA-seq of FACS-sorted cells demonstrating suppression of iCAF signature in fibroblasts (Figure 4H-J), and enrichment of neutrophil markers in immune cells (Figure 4I-K). The loss-of-function approach complements the gain-of-function studies.

result: p63-positive PDA cells possess a secretory phenotype that promotes neutrophil migration, which is further enhanced by co-culture with PSCs/iCAFs.
evaluation: Claims C28 and C80 are supported by transwell migration assays showing enhanced neutrophil chemotaxis in response to conditioned media from SUIT2-p63/PSC co-cultures compared to individual cell types (Figure 4M-N). The experimental design appropriately tests the synergistic effect of tumor cells and CAFs.

result: p63 activates inflammation-related pathways and directly regulates expression of pro-inflammatory cytokine genes through enhancer-mediated transcriptional activation.
evaluation: Claims C29-C31 and C42 are supported by GSEA analysis showing activation of inflammatory pathways (Figure 5A-C), identification of top inflammation-related genes regulated by p63 (Figure 5C), and ChIP-seq data demonstrating p63 binding at enhancer elements near these genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D). The integration of transcriptomic and epigenomic data provides strong mechanistic evidence.

result: p63 installs a super-enhancer at the IL1 locus that is responsible for activating IL1A and IL1B expression and enables a >30-fold increase in IL-1α secretion.
evaluation: Claims C32-C33 and C44 are supported by ChIP-seq data showing a p63-induced super-enhancer between IL1A and IL1B (Figure 5E), CRISPR-interference experiments demonstrating that this enhancer is required for IL1A and IL1B expression (Figure 5E-F), and ELISA data showing increased IL-1α secretion (Figure 5H-I). The functional validation of the enhancer strengthens the mechanistic claim.

result: Both IL1A and IL1B are transcriptionally regulated by p63, but only IL-1α is secreted at detectable levels by p63-expressing PDA cells in vitro, likely due to lack of inflammasome activation required for IL-1β secretion.
evaluation: Claims C34-C35, C73-C74 are supported by ELISA experiments detecting IL-1α but not IL-1β in conditioned media from p63-expressing cells (Figure 5G-I), and the reduction of IL-1α secretion following p63 knockout or enhancer inactivation. The explanation regarding inflammasome activation is supported by citation to established knowledge (Di Paolo and Shayakhmetov, 2016).

result: p63-expressing PDA cells induce an iCAF phenotype via paracrine IL-1α signaling through an IL-1 receptor-dependent mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C36, C43, and C75 are supported by conditioned media experiments using IL-1 receptor knockout PSCs, which show that iCAF marker induction by SUIT2-p63 conditioned media is abolished in the absence of IL-1 receptor (Figure 5J-K). This provides strong evidence for the IL-1-dependent signaling mechanism.

result: In human PDA patient samples, p63 expression correlates with elevated IL1A expression, increased inflammatory gene expression in fibroblasts, and a trend toward increased neutrophil infiltration.
evaluation: Claims C37-C40 are supported by analysis of three independent bulk transcriptome datasets showing elevated IL1A in TP63high samples (Figure 6A), single-cell RNA-seq data demonstrating higher inflammatory gene expression in fibroblasts from TP63high patients (Figure 6D), and multiplex immunofluorescence showing a trend toward increased neutrophil infiltration (Figure 6E-F). The convergence of multiple independent datasets strengthens the clinical relevance.

result: p63 serves as a functional biomarker identifying a poor prognostic subgroup of PDA patients with enhanced inflammatory tumor microenvironment.
evaluation: Claims C41 and C57 are supported by the comprehensive in vitro, in vivo, and patient data demonstrating that p63 expression promotes inflammatory changes in the tumor microenvironment. The integration of experimental models with patient data provides strong evidence for p63 as a biomarker, though the prognostic value relies on prior studies showing poor outcomes in squamous-subtype PDA.

result: Ectopic p63 expression enhances PDA cell growth in vivo but not in vitro, as validated in SUIT2 and mM1 organoid models.
evaluation: Claims C16 and C64 are supported by tumor volume measurements showing enhanced growth in vivo (Figure 3A-B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-K) and in vitro proliferation assays showing no growth advantage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D). The in vivo-specific phenotype is validated in multiple models, strengthening the conclusion.

result: MIAPaca2 cells express only the TA isoform of p63 and are of neuroendocrine origin, while KLM1 is the only p63-positive PDA cell line that does not exhibit growth arrest following p63 inactivation in vitro, yet harbors a similar transcriptional and epigenomic profile to other p63-expressing lines.
evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), competition-based GFP depletion assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-H), and GSEA/ChIP-seq data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I-K). These characterizations are important for interpreting the experimental results and are well-supported by the data.

result: p63 expression in orthotopic mM1 tumors correlates with decreased infiltrating CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, consistent with the immunosuppressive effect of tumor-associated neutrophils, and this phenotype is correlated with pre-existing TP63 expression levels in human PDA organoid xenografts.
evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by flow cytometry data showing decreased T cell infiltration in mM1-p63 tumors (Figure 3J-K) and RNA-seq/gene expression data from organoid xenografts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q-T). The interpretation is consistent with prior literature on neutrophil-mediated immunosuppression.

result: FACS-sorted fibroblasts from SUIT2-p63 tumors show increased iCAF markers and decreased myCAF markers, reduced neutrophil infiltration in p63 knockout tumors is confirmed by immunofluorescence, and SUIT2-p63 cells augment the iCAF phenotype in co-culture with PSCs.
evaluation: Claims C68-C70 are supported by RT-qPCR data from FACS-sorted fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1N-P), immunofluorescence staining for neutrophil markers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-H), and RT-qPCR analysis of co-cultures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I). These supporting experiments validate the main findings using orthogonal approaches.

result: Conditioned media from p63-expressing PDA cells can promote modest neutrophil recruitment in the absence of co-cultured PSCs through a CXCL1-dependent mechanism.
evaluation: Claim C71 is supported by transwell migration assays with CXCL1 blocking antibody (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K-M). This demonstrates that p63-expressing tumor cells can directly recruit neutrophils, though the effect is enhanced by PSCs/iCAFs.

result: Among p63 target inflammatory genes, IL1A and IL1B are outliers with the most significant expression changes following p63 perturbation.
evaluation: Claim C72 is supported by heatmap analysis showing gene expression changes across multiple cell lines (Figure 5D). This observation motivates the focus on IL-1 signaling in subsequent experiments.

result: The ΔN isoform of TP63 is overexpressed in squamous-subtype PDA tumors, and TP63 expression correlates with SOX2 expression in single-cell RNA-seq analysis of tumor ductal cells.
evaluation: Claims C76-C77 are supported by citation to Bailey et al., 2016 and single-cell RNA-seq data analysis. The correlation with SOX2 is interesting given the role of SOX2 in squamous differentiation in other tumor types.

result: PDA has a five-year survival rate below 10%, and approximately 15% of pancreatic tumors exhibit adenosquamous histology characterized by aberrant expression of squamous lineage markers, which is associated with poor clinical outcomes. Squamous cells are not normally present in the human pancreas.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 establish the clinical and biological context for the study and are supported by citations to established literature. These background claims are well-documented in the field.

result: p63 (ΔN isoform) is the master regulator of the adenosquamous phenotype in PDA, binding to thousands of genomic sites to drive squamous lineage gene expression, and is both necessary and sufficient for this transcriptional program. p63 induction leads to enhanced motility, invasion, and chemotherapy resistance.
evaluation: Claims C5-C8 summarize prior work from the authors and others establishing p63 as the master regulator of squamous differentiation in PDA. These claims are supported by citations to multiple studies and provide the foundation for the current work.

result: Inflammation drives PDA progression, with neutrophils suppressing anti-tumor immunity and correlating with aggressive disease. iCAFs produce high levels of inflammatory cytokines including IL-6, CXCL1, and LIF.
evaluation: Claims C9-C11 establish the importance of inflammation and CAF heterogeneity in PDA and are supported by citations to established literature. These background claims motivate the investigation of p63's role in stromal inflammation.

result: IL-1/JAK/STAT signaling is the key pathway for iCAF formation in PDA, many p63-regulated genes correspond to NF-κB targets, and NF-κB is constitutively active in pancreatic cancer requiring an IL-1α-driven feed-forward loop. Maintenance of inflamed CAF state depends on NF-κB signaling.
evaluation: Claims C45-C50 integrate the current findings with prior literature on IL-1, NF-κB, and CAF biology. These claims are supported by citations to relevant studies and help contextualize the mechanistic findings.

result: p63 promotes expression of other pro-inflammatory cytokines (CXCL1, GM-CSF) implicated in PDA progression, and associations between squamous cell carcinomas and inflammatory infiltrates have been observed in other tumor contexts, including lung adenocarcinoma where SOX2 promotes inflammation through CXCL5.
evaluation: Claims C51-C54 place the findings in the broader context of squamous differentiation and inflammation across tumor types. These claims are supported by RNA-seq data and citations to relevant literature.

result: Squamous cells of the epidermis express high levels of IL-1α at steady state, IL1A is a key p63 target in normal keratinocytes, and the normal squamous epithelium serves as a protective barrier requiring tightly regulated inflammatory pathways. Amplified inflammation may be an inevitable consequence of squamous trans-differentiation in diverse tumor contexts.
evaluation: Claims C55-C56, C78, C84-C85 provide biological context for why squamous differentiation might be inherently linked to inflammation. These claims are supported by citations to established literature and logical inference from the normal function of squamous epithelium.

result: Monoclonal antibodies targeting IL-1α/β and the IL-1 receptor antagonist Anakinra have shown promise as cancer therapies, suggesting that squamous-subtype PDA patients may benefit from anti-inflammatory therapies and IL-1 targeting agents may show efficacy in appropriately stratified patients.
evaluation: Claims C58-C59 are supported by citations to prior studies, but claims C86-C87 are speculative regarding therapeutic implications. While the mechanistic findings support the rationale for IL-1 targeting in p63-positive PDA, clinical efficacy has not been demonstrated. The therapeutic potential requires prospective clinical validation.

result: Adenosquamous carcinoma is defined by >15% squamous differentiation, p63 may function as an amplifier of NF-κB transcriptional output, the pro-tumorigenic effects of CXCL1 and GM-CSF would be amplified by IL-1α-mediated crosstalk, and inflammation is generally associated with squamous lineage tumors through multiple mechanisms.
evaluation: Claim C79 is supported by established histopathological definitions. Claims C81-C83 are reasonable inferences based on the data and prior literature, but represent interpretations rather than directly demonstrated findings. The proposed amplification mechanisms are plausible but would benefit from additional experimental validation.
